courses.title: Plan Your App Measurement
courses.homeBlurb: Decide what to track and why.

lessons.title: Map the user journey
lessons.heading: Start with the path your users take.
lessons.intro: Before naming any events, sketch the key steps a new user moves through — from install to the moment they get real value.

example.label: Shopping app
example.title: Install → Browse → Add to cart → Purchase
example.text: Four steps describe the core journey. Each one is a candidate for measurement.

steps: The first screen a new user sees
The steps between install and value
Where users most often drop off
lessons.yourTurn: List the 4–6 steps of your core journey in the event tracking plan.

lessons.title: Define your activation event
lessons.heading: Choose the action that represents value.
lessons.intro: An activation event should reflect a meaningful first experience in your app. Choose it around the value your app delivers.

example.label: Shopping app
example.title: First purchase completed
example.text: For this example, the first completed purchase is the activation event.

steps: The conditions that make it count
The event name you will track
lessons.yourTurn: Use the event tracking plan to define one activation event for your app.

lessons.title: Create an event plan
lessons.heading: Turn your journey into a tracking plan.
lessons.intro: A good event plan lists each event, when it fires, and the parameters that explain it. Keep names consistent and readable.

example.label: Shopping app
example.title: add_to_cart · item_id, price, currency
example.text: One event, three parameters — enough to answer “what did people add, and how much was it worth?”

steps: The parameters you need to analyse it
lessons.yourTurn: Add at least five events with triggers and parameters to your plan.

lessons.title: Check event quality
lessons.heading: Make sure your data can be trusted.
lessons.intro: Before you rely on a report, check that events fire once, at the right moment, with the right values.

example.label: Shopping app
example.title: purchase fired twice per order
example.text: Duplicate events inflate revenue. A quick debug session catches this before launch.

lessons.yourTurn: Run through your app in debug mode and tick off each event in the plan.

courses.title: Understand Your App Funnel
courses.blurb: Learn how Firebase Analytics uses events.
courses.homeBlurb: Turn app events into useful questions.

lessons.title: Events in Firebase
lessons.heading: Everything in Firebase starts with an event.
lessons.intro: Firebase records what users do as events with parameters. Automatic events cover the basics; custom events cover your product.

example.label: Fitness app
example.title: workout_started
example.text: A custom event that tells you how many users actually begin a workout.

lessons.yourTurn: Map your planned events into the Firebase event map.

lessons.title: Build a funnel
lessons.heading: Line up the steps that lead to value.
lessons.intro: A funnel shows how many users move from one step to the next, and where they stop.

example.label: Fitness app
example.title: Open → Start workout → Finish workout
example.text: A three-step funnel shows the biggest drop is between start and finish.

steps: The first step of the funnel
lessons.yourTurn: Sketch a three-step funnel for your app.

lessons.title: Use audiences
lessons.heading: Group users by what they did.
lessons.intro: Audiences let you segment users by behaviour and use those groups in reports and campaigns.

example.label: Fitness app
example.title: Started but never finished
example.text: An audience you can re-engage with a helpful reminder.

steps: The behaviour that defines the group
What you will do with the audience
lessons.yourTurn: Define one audience you would act on this month.

lessons.title: Ask better questions
lessons.heading: Turn reports into decisions.
lessons.intro: The best analytics work starts from a question, not a dashboard.

example.label: Fitness app
example.title: Why do users stop after day 3?
example.text: A specific question points you to the right report.

lessons.yourTurn: Write down three questions your funnel should answer.

courses.title: Plan a Re-engagement Journey
courses.blurb: Know who to bring back and why.

lessons.title: Pick the audience
lessons.heading: Know who you want to bring back.
lessons.intro: Re-engagement works best when it targets a clear group with a clear reason to return.

example.label: News app
example.title: Readers inactive for 14 days
example.text: A specific window keeps the message relevant.

steps: How long they have been away
lessons.yourTurn: Define one lapsed audience in the journey planner.

lessons.title: Choose the channel
lessons.heading: Meet users where they are.
lessons.intro: Push, email and in-app messages each fit a different moment.

example.label: News app
example.title: Email for weekly digest
example.text: Inactive users may have disabled push; email can still reach them.

steps: The channels you have permission for
The channel that fits the message
lessons.yourTurn: Pick a primary and fallback channel for your audience.

lessons.title: Write the message
lessons.heading: Give a reason to return.
lessons.intro: A good message reminds users of value, not of your app.

example.label: News app
example.title: “3 stories you missed on topics you follow”
example.text: Personal and specific beats generic.

steps: The value you are reminding them of
lessons.yourTurn: Draft two message variants.

lessons.title: Measure the result
lessons.heading: Know if it worked.
lessons.intro: Compare returning users against a holdout group to see the true lift.

example.label: News app
example.title: 10% holdout
example.text: A small control group shows what would have happened anyway.

lessons.yourTurn: Set a metric and holdout for your journey.

lessons.title: Ask for permission well
lessons.heading: Earn the opt-in.
lessons.intro: Explain the value of notifications before showing the system prompt.

example.label: Travel app
example.title: “Get gate changes instantly”
example.text: A pre-prompt tied to a real benefit lifts opt-in rates.

steps: What happens if they say no
lessons.yourTurn: Write a pre-permission message.

lessons.title: Write the message
lessons.heading: One message, one action.
lessons.intro: Short, specific notifications get opened.

example.label: Travel app
example.title: “Your flight boards in 30 min — Gate B12”
example.text: Useful, timely and actionable.

lessons.yourTurn: Draft a message in the push worksheet.

lessons.title: Choose the timing
lessons.heading: Send at the right moment.
lessons.intro: Timing based on behaviour beats a fixed schedule.

example.label: Travel app
example.title: 24h before departure
example.text: Triggered by the trip, not the calendar.

lessons.yourTurn: Set a trigger and frequency cap.

lessons.title: Review performance
lessons.heading: Learn from opens and opt-outs.
lessons.intro: Watch opt-outs as closely as opens.

example.label: Travel app
example.title: Opt-outs spike after promo pushes
example.text: A signal to keep promos rare.

lessons.yourTurn: Pick the three metrics you will review weekly.

lessons.title: Set the objective
lessons.heading: Decide what success means.
lessons.intro: Installs, activations and revenue each lead to different campaign choices.

example.label: Game app
example.title: Optimise for day-7 retained players
example.text: A deeper goal than installs.

lessons.yourTurn: Write the objective section of the campaign brief.

lessons.title: Define the audience
lessons.heading: Know who you are trying to reach.
lessons.intro: Describe your ideal user in terms platforms can target.

example.label: Game app
example.title: Puzzle fans, 25–44, Android
example.text: Specific enough to guide creative and bids.

lessons.yourTurn: Describe your audience in the brief.

lessons.title: Plan the creative
lessons.heading: Show the value fast.
lessons.intro: The first two seconds of a video ad decide most outcomes.

example.label: Game app
example.title: Gameplay in the first second
example.text: Show, don’t tell.

lessons.yourTurn: List three creative concepts.

lessons.title: Measure and iterate
lessons.heading: Learn from every campaign.
lessons.intro: Connect ad data to in-app events so you can see true performance.

example.label: Game app
example.title: Cost per retained player
example.text: A metric that matches the objective.

lessons.yourTurn: Set your review cadence.

courses.title: Design a Deep-link Journey
courses.blurb: Connect a click to an app destination.

lessons.title: Deep link basics
lessons.heading: Send users to the right screen.
lessons.intro: A deep link opens a specific place in your app instead of the home screen.

example.label: Shopping app
example.title: myapp://product/123
example.text: Opens the exact product from an email or ad.

lessons.yourTurn: List three destinations you want to link to.

lessons.title: Deferred deep links
lessons.heading: Keep the context through install.
lessons.intro: Deferred deep links remember the destination when a user installs first.

example.label: Shopping app
example.title: Ad → Store → Install → Product
example.text: The user lands on the product they clicked.

lessons.yourTurn: Map both paths in the deep link journey map.

lessons.title: Fallbacks
lessons.heading: Plan for when things fail.
lessons.intro: Every link needs a sensible fallback.

example.label: Shopping app
example.title: Web product page
example.text: Desktop users still see the product.

lessons.yourTurn: Add a fallback for each destination.

lessons.title: Test the journey
lessons.heading: Click every link before launch.
lessons.intro: Test on real devices, installed and not installed.

example.label: Shopping app
example.title: Fresh install test
example.text: The case most often missed.

lessons.yourTurn: Run the five tests and record the results.

courses.title: Create a Consistent UTM System
courses.homeBlurb: Give your campaigns a shared naming language.

lessons.title: Why UTMs matter
lessons.heading: Know where traffic comes from.
lessons.intro: UTM parameters tag links so analytics tools can group traffic by source and campaign.

example.label: Newsletter
example.title: utm_source=newsletter
example.text: One parameter, a clear answer.

lessons.yourTurn: List the channels your team uses today.

lessons.title: Naming rules
lessons.heading: Agree on one language.
lessons.intro: Lowercase, hyphens and a fixed vocabulary keep reports clean.

example.label: Paid social
example.title: paid-social, not Paid_Social
example.text: Consistent casing avoids split rows.

lessons.yourTurn: Write your rules in the UTM naming template.

lessons.title: Build links
lessons.heading: Make it easy to do the right thing.
lessons.intro: A shared builder prevents typos.

example.label: Launch
example.title: One sheet, one builder
example.text: Everyone builds links the same way.

lessons.yourTurn: Build three links using your template.

lessons.title: Govern over time
lessons.heading: Keep the system clean.
lessons.intro: Review new values monthly and retire old ones.

example.label: Team
example.title: Monthly UTM review
example.text: Fifteen minutes keeps reports trustworthy.

lessons.yourTurn: Assign an owner and a review date.

posts.author: NH
posts.name: Sample member
posts.title: Which events should we track before launch?
posts.body: I am mapping signup, onboarding and first purchase. How would you define activation?

replies.author: OA
replies.text: Start with the moment users first get value — for us it was the first saved item, not signup.

replies.author: SK
replies.text: Keep the launch list short. 8–10 well-named events beat 50 noisy ones.

posts.author: OA
posts.name: Sample member
posts.title: How do you test a deferred deep link?
posts.body: What should we check when the app is installed and when it is not?

replies.author: MA
replies.text: Delete the app, clear the browser, click the link, install from the store, then open. Repeat on both platforms.

posts.author: SK
posts.name: Sample member
posts.title: How should we name UTMs across channels?
posts.body: We want consistent source, medium and campaign values across our team.

posts.author: MA
posts.name: Sample member
posts.title: What belongs in a first-week retention journey?
posts.body: How would you sequence reminders without repeating the same message?

replies.author: NH
replies.text: Day 1 value reminder, day 3 feature tip, day 6 social proof. Each message teaches something new.

posts.author: RL
posts.name: Sample member
posts.title: A pre-permission screen doubled our push opt-in
posts.body: We explained the value before the system prompt. Opt-in went from 31% to 64%.

posts.author: JT
posts.name: Sample member
posts.title: Our event naming checklist
posts.body: snake_case, verb_object, no PII, and every event has an owner. Saved us hours of clean-up.
